title: INDIA — 1857
subtitle: The Indian Rebellion of 1857
tagline: Experience history through the people who lived it.
description: Explore the events and social conditions surrounding one of the major upheavals in nineteenth-century India.

importantEvents: The introduction of the new Enfield rifle sparked fears of greased cartridges that offended religious practice — a documented grievance among sepoys of the Bengal Army.
Mangal Pandey, a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, attacked his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and was executed days later.
On 10 May 1857, sepoys of the Meerut cantonment rose, released imprisoned comrades, and marched overnight to Delhi — the point at which scattered tension became a regional upheaval.
At Delhi, sepoys turned to the ageing Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, who was proclaimed leader from the Red Fort in mid-May 1857.
Uprisings and sieges followed across the Gangetic plain — at Lucknow, Kanpur and Jhansi — before the British re-captured these centres during late 1857 and early 1858.
On 1 November 1858, Queen Victoria's Proclamation transferred rule from the East India Company to the British Crown.
majorRegions: The North-Western Provinces (today's western Gangetic plain and around Delhi)
Awadh (Oudh), annexed by the East India Company in 1856
The Doab and the towns along the Ganga-Yamuna corridor
Bundelkhand and central India around Jhansi
socialGroups: Sepoys of the Bengal Army — the backbone of the Company's fighting force
Peasant cultivators across the Gangetic countryside
Artisans and weavers in towns hit hard by changing trade
Merchants and traders whose routes ran through the disrupted region
Zamindars, taluqdars and local authorities caught between orders and uprisings
The last Mughal court at Delhi and princely rulers across India
context: The East India Company controlled vast territory. Its Bengal Army's Indian soldiers outnumbered its British soldiers many times over.
Hard-fought revenue collection, annexation of states, and changes to land rights created deep rural grievances long before any cartridge.
Scientific, ritual, and religious sensitivities — real and rumoured — turned army reform into a source of mistrust.
News travelled unevenly. People far from the fighting knew only rumours, which shaped what they did as much as facts did.
Most people in the region did not fight battles. They lived through the upheaval — planting, hiding, trading, fleeing and rebuilding.

title: MAHARASHTRA — 17TH CENTURY
subtitle: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
subjectDescription: Explore the rise of Swarajya through events, places and the people who experienced them.
tagline: A homeland, built fort by fort.
description: The seventeenth century saw the rise of Swarajya in the Maratha country of the Western Ghats and the Deccan: a new power, born from hill forts and valley loyalties, that challenged the Sultanates of Bijapur and Ahmadnagar and then the Mughal empire itself.

importantEvents: Shivaji was born at Shivneri Fort, by tradition in February 1630, to Jijabai and Shahaji Bhonsle.
Through the 1640s he gathered the mavals — the martial hill people of the valleys around Pune — and began taking the forts of the ghats, beginning with Torna (c. 1646).
Rajgad became the capital stronghold from about 1648–49, the workshop of the growing state.
On 10 November 1659, at Pratapgad, Bijapur's general Afzal Khan was killed in a meeting with Shivaji and his army routed.

After the siege of Panhala and the escape at Ghod Khind (1660), and a risky journey to the Mughal court at Agra and escape (1666), Swarajya resumed expansion along the Konkan coast and into the south.
On 6 June 1674, Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad — the public assertion of a sovereign Maratha state.
majorRegions: The hill forts of the Sahyadri — Shivneri, Torna, Rajgad, Sinhagad, Pratapgad, Panhala
The Deccan plateau around Pune and Satara
The Konkan coast and its ports
Surat on the Gujarat coast, the great Mughal port (raided in 1664)
The imperial city of Agra (episode of 1666)
socialGroups: The mavals — the hill communities who supplied the first soldiers
Maratha service nobles and captains holding forts across the country
Cultivators of the Deccan and Konkan who paid revenue to whoever held the land
Artisans building and supplying the new fortresses
Merchants of the Konkan and Surat caught between competing powers
The Sultanates of Bijapur and Ahmadnagar and the Mughal empire — the rival powers of the Deccan
context: The Deccan of the 1600s was divided among the Sultanates and, increasingly, the Mughal empire; Maratha warlords held estates under them.
Fortresses in the ghat country were the decisive instruments: they commanded passes, valleys, revenue and loyalty.
Swarajya — self-rule — was both a political demand and a way of organising a homeland, built around forts, oaths and local loyalties.
The movement learned to balance war and diplomacy, patience and audacity, especially between treaty with the Mughals and renewed resistance.
